title: Cheryl Lerena
dek: The verse of David's mother, gathered out of the documents it was buried in and set as poetry for the first time.
living: **Cheryl Lerena is living.** This archive's rule for the living is **name only** — no dates, no places of residence, no photographs — and that rule is kept here. What is published is **her work**, at her son's request, and nothing about her life.
lead:
The writing was not filed as poetry. It was found **inside other documents** — a memorial address, a letter to a sister — set as ordinary paragraphs in the middle of prose, in capitals, in a Word file from 2000. Nobody had ever taken it out and looked at it as verse.

That is the whole purpose of this page. **Two poems, and one of them is certainly hers.**

poems.title: I had a darling sister
poems.occasion: Written for the **first anniversary** of her sister's death, and read to the family. **Catherine Tersia Lerena, called Rene, 21 May 1952 – 30 September 1999.**
poems.conf: doc — signed by her at the foot of the document it stands in
text: A dream her life was not
She knew pain as her friend
poems.note: Nine lines, no rhyme, no punctuation to speak of, and it ends on an ellipsis rather than a full stop — the same trailing dots she uses all through the prose around it, as though the sentence could not be finished. **«She knew pain as her friend»** is the line the poem turns on. It is not a comfort and it does not try to be.

poems.title: If love could change the way things are
poems.occasion: Stands a few paragraphs below the first, in the same memorial address.
text: If love could change the way things are
You would live forever and go so far
You'd know that I am always there
That I'll always love you, I'll always care
poems.note: Four lines, rhymed **aabb**, and it sits immediately before the sentence *«In October of 1992 a card arrived in the mail … here it is, I will share it with you»*. So it may be hers, or it may be **the verse off that card**, quoted. The document does not say, and this archive will not decide for it. **It is printed here as uncertain rather than claimed as hers or dropped for being awkward.**

excluded.heading: One poem that is not hers, and is not printed
excluded.text:
A third piece of verse sits in a letter she wrote to her surviving sister in **November 1999**, six weeks after Rene died. It opens *«Life is a sojourn here on earth»* and runs eighteen lines.

**It is not Cheryl's.** It is by **Helen Steiner Rice**, the American writer of devotional verse whose poems were printed on greeting cards by the million through the second half of the twentieth century — which is almost certainly how it reached a Johannesburg letterbox. It is **still in copyright** and it is **not published here**.

It is mentioned because leaving it out silently would be its own kind of error. **A woman quoting a poem in a letter about her dead sister is not the author of it**, and an archive that prints everything it finds in a folder ends up attributing greeting cards to grieving people.

rest.heading: What else is in the folder, and why it is not here
rest.text:
The poems came out of a much larger body of writing — roughly **forty pieces**: memorial addresses, a fiftieth-birthday speech, diaries kept for two grandsons, a letter written **to an unborn child**, and some thirty-five letters to children and grandchildren for birthdays, Christmases, first days of school and journeys abroad.

**None of it is published**, and none of it is quoted here. It was written **to named living people**, most of it in a folder assembled for them to read one day, and it is theirs and hers rather than the archive's. Two documents in the same folder are excluded permanently and absolutely: a **statement of allegations** naming living people, and an unrelated **court judgment** that has nothing to do with this family.

If more of the writing is to be published, **it is Cheryl's to release, piece by piece.** This page will take whatever she gives it.

lerena.heading: The Lerena side, which this archive has barely begun
lerena.text:
The surname on this page is the one the archive knows least. **Lerena** comes in through David's mother, and against the Defranceschi spine — nine generations, registers to 1644 — it is nearly blank. The DNA says the same thing from the other direction: the maternal side is **Dutch, Scottish, Welsh, Irish and English by descent, and southern African by residence**, with a strand running to Argentina, and this project has written almost nothing about any of it.

What it has, at the moment, is **her**. These few lines of verse and the names inside them — a sister, a mother, a brother — are currently the archive's **best single source** on the Lerena family, which says less about the poems than about how much work is still owed to that half of the story.

source: From the family's own document folder, read 10 September 2026 at David's request. «I had a darling sister» and «If love could change the way things are» are transcribed from the memorial address for Catherine Tersia Lerena, first anniversary, September 2000; the same two also stand in an earlier draft of the same document. Line breaks are as they fall in the originals. Spelling and the trailing ellipses are hers and are not corrected.
